source_text: CAPUT VIGESIMUM SECUNDUM, De DEO PATRE. Pater est prima persona in sacrosancta Trinitate, quae sermonem suum aeternum gignit, et una cum Filio Spiritum sanctum spirat. Pater dicitur non tropice sed proprie. Sicut enim proprie est, vivit, intelligit, vult, agit: ita et proprie gignit, etsi non ita gignat ut res corporeae. Hinc sapienter Basilius Magnus libro I contra Eunomium: nullum potius et majus dogma quam in Patrem et in Filium fidem evangelio nostrae salutis inesse arbitror.
english: CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO. On God the Father.

The Father is the first person in the most holy Trinity, who begets His eternal Word, and together with the Son spirates the Holy Spirit. He is called Father not tropically but properly. For just as He properly is, lives, understands, wills, acts: so also He properly begets, though He does not beget as bodily things do.
Hence wisely Basil the Great in book 1 against Eunomius: I judge that no dogma is more important and greater than that faith in the Father and in the Son is in the gospel of our salvation.

source_text: II. Sunt autem hic quaedam utiles observationes et regulae. 1. Prima persona proprie, non tropice dicitur Pater. 2. Persona Patris tribus modis consideranda est. Absolute in sese, quia est omnis originis expers, sive spectemus secundum essentiam, sive secundum subsistendi modum. In ordine ad Filium, quem in communi essentia ex perfectione sua splendentem in Filio gignit actu interno et aeterno. In ordine ad Spiritum sanctum, quem una cum Filio in communi essentia spirat ex perfectione tum sua, tum Filii resplendente in Spiritu sancto. 3. Genitura, qua Deus Pater Filium ab aeterno genuit, plusquam toto genere differt ab omni genitura physica. Nam in rebus physicis est transiens, in divinis purus actus immanens. Neque in his locum habet sectio, vel extensio, vel propagatio et multiplicatio, vel derivatio et transfusio aut effusio.
english: II. But here there are certain useful observations and rules. 1. The first person is called Father properly, not tropically.

2. The person of the Father is to be considered in three ways. Absolutely in Himself, because He is devoid of every origin, whether we regard according to essence or according to mode of subsisting. In order to the Son, whom in the common essence shining from His perfection in the Son He begets by an internal and eternal act. In order to the Holy Spirit, whom together with the Son in the common essence He spirates from the perfection both of His own and of the Sons shining in the Holy Spirit.

3. The begetting by which God the Father begot the Son from eternity differs more than in whole genus from every physical begetting. For in physical things it is transient; in divine things it is pure immanent act. Nor has place here section, or extension, or propagation and multiplication, or derivation and transfusion or effusion.

source_text: Neque tamen hoc arcanum in sola speculatione positum est, sicuti in intellectus nostri operatione genera et species concipiuntur, sed cessante etiam intellectus nostri operatione, vera est hypostaseon multiplicatio, veraque earum distinctio, citra ullam inter se confusionem aut separationem. Hujus igitur generationis modum ad humanae nativitatis aut ullius creatae rei leges revocare, ineptum, impium, imo sacrilegum est. Quapropter, qui caute et circumspecte loqui amant, quasdam veterum kyriologias vitant, quales sunt: divinam essentiam gignere vel gigni; essentiam gignere personam; Deum ex sua essentia gignere Deum. Vere autem et proprie dicitur, Patrem genuisse Filium, personam personam, hypostasin hypostasin, non ex essentia, sed in unitate essentiae, quam Pater Filio totam dedit, non alienatione, sed communicatione. CAPUT VIGESIMUM TERTIUM, De FILIO, sequitur.
english: Yet this secret is not placed in speculation alone, as genera and species are conceived in our intellects operation, but even when our intellects operation ceases, there is a true multiplication of hypostases, and a true distinction of them, without any confusion or separation among themselves.

Therefore to reduce the mode of this generation to the laws of human nativity or of any created thing is inept, impious, even sacrilegious. Therefore those who love to speak cautiously and circumspectly avoid certain of the ancients kyriologies, such as: the divine essence begets or is begotten; essence begets a person; God from His essence begets God.

But truly and properly it is said that the Father has begotten the Son, person a person, hypostasis a hypostasis, not from essence but in the unity of essence, which the Father gave wholly to the Son, not by alienation but by communication. CHAPTER TWENTY-THREE, On the SON, follows.
